subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: Monday. Maria, five, pushed Simran off the swing. The teacher frowned, and Maria went pale. "Am I bad now? Will I get a punishment?" Wednesday. Simran grabbed Maria's crayon. Maria's hand went up, then she looked at the teacher's desk and dropped it. "No hitting," she whispered. "Teacher gets angry." Friday. At home, Nani asked Maria why hitting is wrong. "Because you get punished," Maria said firmly. "That's the rule." "And if nobody saw?" Maria thought very hard, swinging her legs. "Then it's still the rule, Nani. Rules are just there."

qa.q: What did Maria do on Monday?
qa.a: She pushed Simran off the swing.

qa.q: What was Maria worried about when the teacher frowned?
qa.a: She worried she was bad now and that she would get a punishment.

qa.q: What choice did Maria make on Wednesday, and what was it based on?
qa.a: She dropped her raised hand instead of hitting Simran, because she expected the teacher to get angry.

qa.q: What might change if Nani asked Maria how Simran felt after the push?
qa.a: Maria might begin to notice that hitting hurts Simran, not only that it makes adults angry.

grounding: A five-year-old explains that hitting is wrong because you get punished and treats the rule as simply there, judging right by adult anger.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: Rain kept the whole kindergarten indoors, and the teacher had stepped out to fetch towels. Omkar snatched Hemant's toy truck. Hemant's fist came up. Then he looked at the door. It was empty. He still stopped. "Hitting is bad," he told Omkar in a loud whisper. "Why?" said Omkar. "'Cause Miss gets angry and you sit in the corner chair." "But Miss isn't here." Hemant's forehead crinkled. He looked at the door again, then at the corner chair, as if the chair itself might tell on him. "The corner knows," he said, and put both hands behind his back.

qa.q: Why had the teacher stepped out?
qa.a: To fetch towels.

qa.q: What does Hemant's look at the corner chair suggest he felt?
qa.a: He seemed afraid of punishment even with Miss away, as if the corner chair itself could catch him.

qa.q: What could Miss do when she comes back to build on Hemant's choice?
qa.a: She could praise him for keeping his hands back and ask how Omkar might feel if hit, so his reason grows beyond the corner chair.

qa.q: Why might Omkar question Hemant's reason?
qa.a: Omkar noticed Miss was not in the room, so the threat of the corner seemed empty to Omkar.

grounding: A kindergartner holds back from hitting because the teacher gets angry and the corner punishes, treating the rule as a fixed fact even when no adult is present.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: Kiran, five, came up three floors in the lift, crying. "Salma hit me! Ammi, she's very bad now. Watchman uncle will tell her mummy and she'll get a big scolding." Ammi wiped his face with her dupatta. "Is hitting wrong only because of the scolding?" Kiran looked at her as if she had asked why the sky was up. "Hitting is wrong because you get punished, Ammi. Everybody knows." "And if nobody scolded her?" He thought about it, then shook his head. "Somebody always scolds."

qa.q: Who did Kiran say would tell Salma's mummy?
qa.a: Watchman uncle.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel about Ammi's question, judging by his look?
qa.a: He was puzzled by it, as if the rule about hitting were as plain a fact as the sky being up.

qa.q: What could Ammi try next to help Kiran look beyond the scolding?
qa.a: She could ask how the hit felt to him, so he links hitting with hurt rather than only with punishment.

qa.q: What would change if Ammi had simply promised to get Salma scolded?
qa.a: Kiran would learn even more firmly that right and wrong depend on an adult's anger, instead of starting to think about why hitting hurts.

grounding: A five-year-old says hitting is wrong because you get punished and cannot imagine a world where no one scolds, treating the rule as a fact.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
"Dadi, Chintu hit me with the spoon!"
Urmila Dadi looked up from the peas. "And what did you do, Sumit?"
"Nothing. I didn't hit back." He puffed out his chest. "Hitting is bad."
"Why is it bad?"
"Because Mummy gets angry. And then no cartoons."
"What if Mummy is at the office?"
Sumit frowned hard. "Then... still bad. Still no cartoons. Later."
"And Chintu? He's only two."
"He'll get a big scolding when he's big," Sumit said, very sure. "That's the rule."
Dadi pulled him onto her lap. "Show me your arm. Does it hurt where the spoon went?"

qa.q: What did Chintu hit Sumit with?
qa.a: Chintu hit him with the spoon.

qa.q: Why does Sumit think hitting is bad?
qa.a: He thinks it is bad because Mummy gets angry and the cartoons stop, so right and wrong mean whether a grown-up will be cross.

qa.q: What could Dadi try next to help Sumit look beyond the scolding?
qa.a: Asking about his sore arm is a good start; she could gently link it to how the spoon hurt, so hitting is wrong because it hurts someone.

qa.q: How might Chintu, who is only two, understand the rule Sumit is so sure about?
qa.a: At two, Chintu probably has no idea there is a rule at all, so Sumit's certainty about a future scolding means nothing to him yet.

grounding: A five-year-old judges hitting wrong because Mummy gets angry and cartoons stop, treating the rule as a fixed fact.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Nursery note, Tuesday. Written by Neelam, class teacher.
At water time Swati, four, saw Dev push Mahi off the bench. She ran to me first. "Dev did pushing! Now you will be angry?" I asked why pushing is wrong. She thought hard. "Because teacher gets angry. And no star." When I asked what if I hadn't seen, she looked puzzled, as if a rule simply is, like rain.
Later she checked my face before taking her turn on the slide.
Next step: at circle time I'll ask the children how Mahi felt, and read the story about the hurt rabbit. I mentioned it to her mother at pickup; this is very usual at four.

qa.q: What did Swati say would happen because of the pushing?
qa.a: She said the teacher gets angry and there would be no star.

qa.q: What does Swati's puzzled look suggest about how she sees rules?
qa.a: It suggests she feels a rule simply is, like rain, and hasn't thought that pushing could be wrong even if no teacher saw it.

qa.q: How could Neelam support Swati at circle time?
qa.a: By asking how Mahi felt and reading the hurt-rabbit story, Neelam can help Swati link pushing to someone getting hurt, not only to an angry teacher.

qa.q: How might Mahi feel if everyone only talked about the teacher being angry?
qa.a: Mahi might feel the fall itself was forgotten, since all the attention went to the rule and not to the one who got pushed. 🥺

grounding: A teacher's note records a four-year-old judging pushing wrong only because the teacher will be angry, treating the rule as a plain fact.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Gautam, five, had hit a boy who took his crayon. Lavanya, the kindergarten teacher, sat him on the bench.
"Gautam, why is hitting wrong?"
"Because you get punished."
"What else?"
"Because Ma'am gets angry." He looked at her face to check.
"What about Rohit? How did he feel?"
Gautam blinked. "He cried," he said. "Then you got angry."
For Gautam, a rule was just how the world worked, like the sun coming up. Lavanya said gently, "Hitting hurts Rohit's body. That's why we don't do it."
Gautam nodded. He was still watching her face.

qa.q: What did Rohit take from Gautam?
qa.a: His crayon.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when he looked at Lavanya's face?
qa.a: He felt anxious about whether she was angry, since for him being wrong meant being punished.

qa.q: How did Lavanya help Gautam look beyond punishment?
qa.a: She asked how Rohit felt and gently explained that hitting hurts Rohit's body, adding a reason beyond anger and punishment.

qa.q: How might Rohit have felt after being hit?
qa.a: He probably felt hurt and upset, crying after losing his crayon and being hit.

grounding: It shows a young child judging hitting wrong because of punishment and an adult's anger, a rule felt as a fact.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Monday. Zainab, five, hit her brother Tushar with a spoon at dinner. Ammi said, "No TV tonight." Zainab cried, "I won't do it again!"
Wednesday. Tushar teased her. Zainab raised her hand to hit, then stopped and looked towards the kitchen. "Ammi will be angry," she whispered, and put her hand down.
Saturday. Ammi was out. Tushar grabbed Zainab's doll. Zainab looked at the closed door. "Ammi's not here," she said slowly, and pushed him. Then she stood still, frightened, as if Ammi might appear anyway.
When Ammi came home, Zainab ran to her. "I pushed Tushar. Are you angry?"

qa.q: What did Ammi say on Monday after the spoon?
qa.a: "No TV tonight."

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling after pushing Tushar on Saturday?
qa.a: She felt frightened, as if Ammi might appear and punish her even though she was out.

qa.q: What could Ammi add when Zainab asks "Are you angry?"
qa.a: She could calmly explain that pushing hurts Tushar, so Zainab starts to think about his feelings, not only about punishment.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel when Zainab pushes him?
qa.a: He might feel hurt, though he also started it by grabbing her doll.

grounding: It shows a young child judging right by whether an adult will be angry, across several days.

passage:
It was pouring, the power was out, and the teacher had gone to fetch the register. Mridul, five, and Imran were at the block corner.
Imran knocked down Mridul's tower. Mridul's fists clenched.
"Hit him," someone whispered. "No one's looking."
Mridul raised his hand. Then he stopped and looked at the door. "Ma'am will know," he said.
"She's not here."
"She'll know," Mridul said, very sure. "Then I'll get the corner."
He put his hand down. Imran, surprised, began rebuilding.
When the teacher came back, Mridul told her at once. "I didn't hit. So no corner, right?"

qa.q: What did Imran knock down?
qa.a: Mridul's tower.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when he looked at the door?
qa.a: He felt worried about punishment, sure the teacher would somehow know and put him in the corner.

qa.q: How could the teacher build on Mridul's choice?
qa.a: She could praise him for not hitting and gently add that hitting hurts Imran, so he starts to think about feelings as well as punishment.

qa.q: How might Imran see Mridul putting his hand down?
qa.a: Imran seemed surprised and relieved, enough to start rebuilding the tower.

grounding: It shows a young child not hitting because the teacher will know and punish him, seeing the rule as a fact.

passage:
It was Holi, and the colony park was full of coloured water. Gautam squirted Siddharth right in the face. Siddharth, five, raised his hand to hit him, then stopped.
"Why didn't you hit him?" his older cousin asked.
"Because hitting is bad," Siddharth said.
"Why is it bad?"
"Because Mumma will shout and I won't get gujiya." He said it like it was the same as saying the sky is blue.
He wiped his face with his sleeve and went to fill his own pichkari.

qa.q: What was Siddharth going to fill?
qa.a: He went to fill his own pichkari.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth stop himself from hitting Gautam?
qa.a: He was afraid Mumma would shout and he wouldn't get gujiya; to him, hitting is bad because of the punishment.

qa.q: How could Siddharth's mother build on his answer?
qa.a: She could praise his stopping and gently add that hitting hurts people, so he starts thinking about others' feelings too.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel if Siddharth had hit him?
qa.a: Gautam would probably feel hurt and upset, and the Holi play might have turned into a fight.

grounding: A child stops himself from hitting because his mother will be angry, judging right by punishment.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
"Shreya, why did you take the Christmas star back from Vijay?" asked the teacher at the playgroup party.
"Because he snatched it. Snatching is naughty."
"Why is snatching naughty?"
Shreya frowned. "Because Ma'am gets angry. And you go in the quiet corner."
"What if Ma'am wasn't looking?"
Shreya thought, eyes wide. "Then... it's still naughty. Because Ma'am might look."
The teacher smiled. "What about how Vijay feels?"
Shreya shrugged. "He should be in the quiet corner."

qa.q: Where does Shreya say you go when you're naughty?
qa.a: In the quiet corner.

qa.q: Why does Shreya think snatching is naughty?
qa.a: She is worried about the teacher getting angry and the quiet corner; to her, a rule is right because breaking it brings punishment.

qa.q: What could the teacher try next to widen Shreya's thinking?
qa.a: Gently ask how Shreya felt when someone took her things, linking rules to feelings, not just punishment.

qa.q: How might Vijay see the argument over the star?
qa.a: Vijay probably just wanted the star and may feel upset that Shreya wants him in the quiet corner.

grounding: A child says snatching is wrong because the teacher will be angry, seeing rules as fixed facts tied to punishment.

passage:
Nursery note, Eid week

Chetan (5) pushed Irfan off the swing today. When I asked him why pushing is wrong, he said, "Because you get a time-out." I asked, "Is it wrong if nobody sees?" He said, "Somebody always sees."
He could not say how Irfan felt, even though Irfan was crying. He only asked if he would miss the Eid sweets.
I sat with both boys and asked Irfan to show Chetan where it hurt. Chetan watched and said, "Sorry, sorry." I will keep pointing out feelings, not only rules.

qa.q: What did Chetan say you get for pushing?
qa.a: He said, "Because you get a time-out."

qa.q: What was Chetan worried about after pushing Irfan?
qa.a: He was worried about punishment, asking if he'd miss the Eid sweets, rather than about Irfan's feelings.

qa.q: What is the note-writer planning, and why does it help?
qa.a: To keep pointing out feelings, not only rules, so Chetan learns that pushing hurts people, not just that it earns time-outs.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel when Chetan says sorry?
qa.a: Irfan might feel a bit comforted, seeing Chetan notice where it hurt.

grounding: A nursery note shows a child who judges pushing as wrong only because of time-outs, and a teacher starting to point him to feelings.

qa.q: Where was Dadi when Kiran's fist went up?
qa.a: At the kitchen door, frying pakoras.

Chand raat. Sumit snatched Asif's green balloon. Asif's hand flew up, then stopped in the air. "No hitting," he said loudly. "Ammi will get angry."

qa.a: Gently add a reason about feelings, like "Hitting hurts, and the cat felt scared too," while still praising him for stopping.
